title: Bloom’s Taxonomy: Match the Learning to the Work

lessons.title: 1. Read the revised taxonomy accurately
lessons.transcript:
Allow 4 minutes. Bloom’s original cognitive taxonomy was published in 1956. This sample uses the 2001 revision associated with Anderson and Krathwohl: Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, and Create. The revision uses action-oriented category names and places Create after Evaluate. Do not silently mix these labels with the original list. University of Illinois Chicago and Iowa State provide background in Sources.

A compact guide: Remember retrieves information; Understand makes meaning; Apply uses a procedure; Analyze examines parts and relationships; Evaluate judges against criteria; Create develops a coherent new product or plan. The revised framework also distinguishes factual, conceptual, procedural, and metacognitive knowledge. A task involves both what knowledge is used and what a learner does with it.

Worked example: recalling the definition of an urgent ticket is Remember; explaining the distinction between urgent and routine is Understand; using a triage rule on a case is Apply. These are different tasks, even if every screen contains the word “priority.”

The taxonomy is a classification aid. Choosing the highest-sounding label does not automatically improve training. In this sample, use the category that best describes the actual performance you need. A routine procedure can appropriately require Apply.

Now it's your turn. A stakeholder asks you to label a routine record-entry task “Create” because it sounds more advanced. What should you do? Pause the video and make your choice in the activity below.

lessons.title: 2. Classify the task, not just its verb
lessons.transcript:
Allow 4 minutes. A verb alone can conceal the thinking required. “Identify” might mean recognizing a memorized definition or separating relevant evidence from irrelevant details in an unfamiliar case. Read the content, conditions, reference materials, novelty, and required reasoning before assigning a category.

Worked example: fictional rule card: tickets blocking the entire team’s login are urgent; a single user’s cosmetic display problem is routine. Selecting priority by executing this rule is Apply. Examining several incident reports to distinguish shared causes from isolated symptoms is Analyze. Judging two escalation proposals against response-time and capacity criteria is Evaluate. Developing a new triage plan with its own coherent workflow is Create.

Knowledge matters too. The exact queue name is factual knowledge. The relationship between impact and urgency is conceptual. How to perform triage is procedural. Recognizing that your own confidence is low and choosing an appropriate checking strategy involves metacognitive knowledge. These dimensions describe the task, not the intelligence or worth of the learner.

Thirty-second check: choose a familiar task and finish “The learner must use ___ knowledge to ___.” If unsure about the category, write the actual evidence you would need to observe before choosing a label.

Now it's your turn. A quiz says “Analyze this term” but asks learners to select its memorized definition. How should you review it? Pause the video and make your choice in the activity below.

lessons.title: 3. Turn an intention into an observable objective
lessons.transcript:
Allow 4 minutes. “Understand triage” communicates a broad intention but does not specify the evidence to collect. For this sample, make three elements explicit: the observable behavior, the conditions under which it happens, and the acceptable standard. Carnegie Mellon’s learning-objective guidance supports writing objectives that point to a performance that can be assessed.

Worked example: “Given the current rule card and four fictional support tickets, assign a priority to each ticket with at least three correct.” Behavior: assign priorities. Condition: four cases and the rule card. Standard: three of four correct. The numbers are illustrative design choices, not a validated safety threshold. A real organization must set standards appropriate to its risks.

Avoid piling incompatible performances into one objective. “List definitions, build an escalation workflow, and motivate colleagues” needs separate evidence. Also avoid false precision: a strict time limit is appropriate only when speed is genuinely part of the job and the measurement is fair.

Drafting pause, 60 seconds: rewrite “Know the handoff process.” Sample response: “Given a fictional handoff and the required-field checklist, identify all missing required elements.” Add a criterion that reflects the use case. Your draft is a self-check, not an automatically verified performance.

Now it's your turn. Which objective is most ready to guide a case-based assessment? Pause the video and make your choice in the activity below.

lessons.title: 4. Align objective, practice, and evidence
lessons.transcript:
Allow 4 minutes. Alignment means the objective names the intended performance, practice prepares learners for it, and assessment elicits evidence of it. Carnegie Mellon’s alignment guidance illustrates why recall-only tests do not establish an analytical objective.

Worked example: objective “Judge an escalation proposal against impact, staffing, and response-time criteria.” Practice: compare two sample proposals, see a worked critique, then judge a third using those criteria. Assessment: select the strongest judgment of a new proposal and its reason. This selected-response assessment samples judgment; an independently written critique would provide additional evidence of the learner’s reasoning.

Misaligned version: the same objective, followed only by a slide defining escalation and a quiz asking for the definition. The problem is not that definitions are useless. They may be necessary preparation. The problem is that the promised performance is never practiced or assessed.

If the objective is Create, choosing somebody else’s plan is insufficient evidence of original production. Ask the learner to produce an artifact and assess it against transparent criteria. Do not claim that the multiple-choice assessment in this sample verifies creation skill; its objectives deliberately focus on classification and selection.

Now it's your turn. Your objective requires producing a new onboarding plan. The test asks learners to pick the best of three finished plans. What is the best revision? Pause the video and make your choice in the activity below.

lessons.title: 5. Review a small curriculum as an L&D partner
lessons.transcript:
Allow 4 minutes. A review can be practical and brief. Start with the work requirement. Read each objective, find its practice, and identify the evidence that would show success. Flag a gap when the assessment cannot support the claim. Use Bloom’s language to explain the mismatch, not to rank people or decorate slides.

Worked example: a manager requests a 20-minute change module for ticket triage. Requirement: use the new rule card correctly. Draft A has six definition screens and a terminology quiz. Draft B has a brief rule explanation, a worked example, two supported cases, a new-case check, and a job aid. Choose B for this requirement. Keep definitions only where they enable the decision. A rollout communication about why the process is changing may still be needed, but communication and demonstrated skill answer different questions.

Review task, 60 seconds: sketch one objective, one practice task, and one assessment task for something you teach. Underline the same required action in all three. Note one tool or reference available during work that should also be available during practice.

Finish by stating the limit of your evidence. Passing a short sample check supports a narrow conclusion about these decisions. It is not a professional credential or proof of full workplace proficiency.

contentFidelity: All source paragraphs narrated; citation tokens omitted from speech. Authoritative source content and assessments remain unchanged.
accessibility: Burned captions plus equivalent VTT and plain transcript. Leave optional VTT track off by default to avoid duplicate visible captions.
qualityLimitations: No human listening audition or end-to-end playback; runtime lacks audio input. Independent ASR, signal analysis, decoded video, sampled frames, source mapping and caption layout checks performed.
distribution: Original synthetic scenarios and original instructional diagrams. No real-person face/voice cloning.
